'''Reginald Henry Roby''' (July 30, 1961 – February 22, 2005) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 16 seasons during the 1980s and 1990s. He played [[college football]] for the [[Iowa Hawkeyes football|Iowa Hawkeyes]] and was recognized as a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]]. He played for the [[Miami Dolphins]], [[Washington Redskins]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Houston Oilers|Houston]]/[[History of the Tennessee Titans|Tennessee Oilers]], and [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the NFL.<ref name="ProFootballReference.com">{{Cite web |title=Reggie Roby Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RobyRe20.htm |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  Roby died of a heart attack at his [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] home in 2005.

'''Reginald Keith Phillips''' (born December 12, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[Chicago Bears]] from 1985 to 1987 and the [[Phoenix Cardinals]] in 1988. He was selected by the Bears in the second round of the [[1985 NFL draft]] with the 49th overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-09 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Phillips played [[college football]] for the [[SMU Mustangs football|SMU Mustangs]]<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/players/profile?id=PHI606955 Reggie Phillips]. NFL.com</ref> and attended [[Yates High School|Jack Yates Senior High School]] in Houston.

Phillips was a member of the [[1985 Chicago Bears season|1985 Bears]] that won [[Super Bowl XX]];<ref>{{Cite web |date=1986-01-27 |title=Bears Trounce Patriots, 46-10, in Super Bowl |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-01-27-mn-540-story.html |access-date=2023-10-31 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> he is best remembered for returning an [[interception]] for a [[touchdown]] in that game.<ref>{{cite web | last=Breech | first=John | title=Super Bowl LIX stats to know: Eagles morph into 1985 Bears during blowout win over Chiefs | website=CBSSports.com | date=2025-02-10 | url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/super-bowl-lix-stats-to-know-eagles-morph-into-1985-bears-during-blowout-win-over-chiefs/ | access-date=2025-06-24}}</ref> He was also a member of the "Shuffling Crew" in the video [[The Super Bowl Shuffle]].

In his 13-year NFL career, McKenzie appeared in 171 games, all but two of those as a starter.

'''Reginald Kinlaw''' (born January 9, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma Sooners]] before  playing in the NFL for the [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland/Los Angeles Raiders]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. He graduated from [[Miami Springs Senior High School]].

Drafted in the final round of the [[1979 NFL draft]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/teams/teamyear.htm?yr=1979&tm=OAK&lg=NFL |title=1979 Oakland Raiders |access-date=30 January 2013 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130123191746/http://databasefootball.com/teams/teamyear.htm?tm=OAK&lg=nfl&yr=1979 |archive-date=23 January 2013 }}</ref> Kinlaw soon worked his way into the rotation on the [[defensive line]]. He went on to become a mainstay at the [[nose tackle]] position, starting on Raider [[Super Bowl]] winners following the [[Super Bowl XV|1980]] and [[Super Bowl XVIII|1983]] seasons. He was considered an unsung hero on those defenses, which featured stars like [[Ted Hendricks]], [[Rod Martin]], [[Matt Millen]], and, later, [[Howie Long]], [[Lyle Alzado]], and [[Greg Townsend]]. Despite being somewhat undersized at 6-2 and 250 pounds, Kinlaw's quickness demanded double teams, freeing up his teammates to make big plays. "Reggie was the REAL hero of our defense! He was so quick, they always had to double-team him. That would allow us, in the secondary, to make plays." - Lester Hayes, CB, Raiders.<ref>Phone call with Lester "The Judge" Hayes. 12/4/18</ref>

Reggie Kinlaw coached the defensive line at the [[Varsity team|varsity]] level at [[Saint Francis High School (La Cañada Flintridge)|St. Francis High School]] in [[La Cañada Flintridge, California|La Cañada, Flintridge, California]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sfhs.net/ourpages/athletics/football_roster.jsp?rn=5572408 |title=St. Francis High School |website=www.sfhs.net |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724062435/http://www.sfhs.net/ourpages/athletics/football_roster.jsp?rn=5572408 |archive-date=2011-07-24}}</ref> He has a daughter Dionne Kinlaw and son Reggie Kinlaw II.  His son Reggie Kinlaw II, also coached the defensive line on the [[Junior Varsity]] level at St. Francis High School. Reggie retired and moved to Las Vegas in 2012. He has been a heavily involved Alumni since the Raiders moved to Vegas.<ref>Phone call with Reggie Kinlaw.</ref>

'''Reginald O'Keith Rogers''' (January 21, 1964 – October 24, 2013) was an American professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] who played four seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Detroit Lions]] ([[1987 Detroit Lions season|1987]]–[[1988 Detroit Lions season|1988]]), [[Buffalo Bills]] ([[1991 Buffalo Bills season|1991]]), and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] ([[1992 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|1992]]).

A consensus [[1986 College Football All-America Team|All-American]] for the [[Washington Huskies football|Washington Huskies]] in [[Seattle]] under head coach [[Don James (American football)|Don James]], Rogers was chosen seventh overall in the [[1987 NFL draft]] by the [[1987 Detroit Lions football team|Lions]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> However, he only played six games of his rookie season due to a slew of emotional problems, even spending time in a counseling center.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20121102094756/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-3855627.html Woes pile up for Lions' Rogers]. [[Chicago Sun-Times]], 1987-11-15.</ref>  His second season in [[1988 Detroit Lions|1988]] ended after only five games when his car struck another vehicle and killed three teenagers early on Thursday, October 20.<ref name=milwsap>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6IhQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=rRIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3278%2C5699527 |work=Milwaukee Sentinel |agency=Associated Press |title=Reggie Rogers charged in crash |date=October 22, 1988 |page=4, part 2 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name=ergwait>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=9vJVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=luEDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6857%2C5510082 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Police wait for arrest of Rogers |date=October 22, 1988 |page=9C}}</ref><ref name=latwoe>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-12-04-sp-1408-story.html |work=Los Angeles Times |last=Wojciechowski |first=Gene |title=One more nightmare: Reggie Rogers, haunted by the past, faces an uncertain future |date=December 4, 1988 |access-date=August 16, 2019}}</ref> He was later found to have a [[blood alcohol content]] of 0.15, the legal limit in Michigan being 0.10 at the time.<ref name="Sentencing">[https://www.nytimes.com/1990/01/17/sports/sports-people-pro-football-former-lion-sentenced.html Former Lion sentenced]. '''Reginald Lee Jones''' (born May 8, 1971) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]]. He played in the NFL for the [[Carolina Panthers]] (1995–1996),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/players/reggiejones/profile?id=JON653228 |title=Reggie Jones |access-date=2009-02-20 |work=NFL.com }}</ref> the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] (1997–1998, 2001),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chargers-stats.com/2000new/jonesreg.html |title=Reggie Jones |access-date=2009-02-20 |publisher=chargers-stats.com/ |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050819055020/http://www.chargers-stats.com/2000new/jonesreg.html |archive-date=August 19, 2005 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/media/misc/all_time_alphabetical_roster.pdf |title=Kansas City Chiefs All-Time Roster |access-date=2009-02-20 |publisher=kcchiefs.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011090133/http://www.kcchiefs.com/media/misc/all_time_alphabetical_roster.pdf |archive-date=October 11, 2007 }}</ref> and the [[San Diego Chargers]] (2000–2001).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chargers-stats.com/2000new/jonesreg.html |title=Reggie Jones |access-date=2009-02-20 |publisher=chargers-stats.com/ |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050819055020/http://www.chargers-stats.com/2000new/jonesreg.html |archive-date=August 19, 2005 }}</ref> He finished his career with the [[Ottawa Renegades]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL), where he caught 28 passes in 2002.

Jones was also a member of the [[LSU Tigers track and field|Tigers track and field]] team.

In track and field, he competed internationally for the United States, performing in the [[triple jump]] qualifiers at the [[1993 World Championships in Athletics]], and placing sixth at both the [[1994 IAAF World Cup]] and [[1993 Summer Universiade]]. At national level, he placed third at the [[USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships]] in [[1993 USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships|1993]] and [[1994 USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships|1994]]. He failed to make the [[1992 Summer Olympics]] team after placing fifth at the [[1992 United States Olympic Trials (track and field)|1992 United States Olympic Trials]]. At the age of eighteen he won the American Junior College triple jump title in 1991. In his collegiate career with the LSU Tigers, he placed second in the triple jump at the [[1993 NCAA Division I Outdoor Track and Field Championships]] as well as coming seventh in the [[long jump]] and leading off the winning [[4 × 100 meters relay]] team alongside [[Glenroy Gilbert]], Chris King and [[Fabian Muyaba]]. The latter marked Louisiana's defence of that title, as Jones, King, Bryant Williams and [[Jason Sanders]] also won the [[NCAA Division I Outdoor Track and Field Championships – Men's 400 meter relay|NCAA 4 × 100 m relay]] in 1992.

'''Reginald McGowan''' (September 25, 1964 – August 26, 2015) was an American [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] who played for the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] at [[Abilene Christian University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McGoRe20.htm | title=Reggie McGowan stats |access-date=February 6, 2024 |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Reggie McGowan, WR |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/reggie-mcgowan/ |access-date=February 6, 2024 |work=Nfl.com}}</ref>

Born in [[Waco, Texas]], McGowan attended [[Axtell High School (Texas)|Axtell High School]] and was a three-sport athlete (football, basketball, track), being an All-District and All-Region selection in football.<ref name="auto">{{Cite news|url=https://wacotrib.com/obituaries/mcgowan-reginald/article_6b23ee82-ca1d-56cd-aa7d-8069525addc7.html|newspaper=[[Waco News-Tribune]]|title=McGowan, Reginald|date=September 3, 2015|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He also earned selection to the Super Cen-Tex team and was chosen as the Class 2A Player of the Year.<ref name="auto"/> McGowan played [[college football]] at [[Ranger Junior College]] for two years before transferring to the [[Abilene Christian Wildcats football|Abilene Christian Wildcats]].<ref name="auto"/>

McGowan set a single-game [[Lone Star Conference]] (LSC) receiving yards record in 1985.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/abilene-reporter-news/140402921/|newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 8, 1985|page=20|title=ACU, HPCU players cited}} {{Open access}}</ref> He was the league's overall receiving leader that year and was named second-team all-conference and honorable mention [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/abilene-reporter-news/140403022/|newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=February 1, 1986|page=31|title=McGowan, Dycus honorable mentions}} {{Open access}}</ref> He also set a school record for single-game [[touchdown]]s that stood for 20 years.<ref name="auto"/> McGowan later played for the [[New York Giants]] as a [[replacement player]] in 1987, catching a 63-yard touchdown on ''[[Monday Night Football]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/abilene-reporter-news/140403194/|newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 9, 1987|page=14|title=When it rains, it pours; just call and ask Giants|author=Pickett, Al}} {{Open access}}</ref>

After his football career, McGowan worked for the [[KWTX-TV|KWTX]] television station.<ref name="auto"/> He died at age 50 in 2015.<ref name="auto"/>
